summary: Grid optimisation, exploration, and the datacenter power crunch make energy both an AI user and AI's binding constraint. Who tracks it: the utility research bodies and DOE are the primary record, with the grid and oilfield incumbents' own technology programs layered on top.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey recorded 12.6% of utilities firms answering yes to using AI in the most recent reference period, down from 17.1% in the prior period. That headline figure covers only the utilities NAICS code, with oil and gas extraction reporting separately under mining, so the broader energy sector's footprint with AI is wider than the single number suggests.

The applications cluster in two distinct parts of the industry. On the grid and renewables side, the Department of Energy's AI office describes work spanning real-time grid balancing, reactor optimization, carbon capture, and grid security, and its Grid Modernization Initiative serves as the federal record of AI projects across those domains. NextEra Energy, described as the largest US renewable producer, uses AI to forecast wind and solar yield, optimize battery dispatch, and automate plant maintenance. The Electric Power Research Institute runs working groups on AI grid resilience, wildfire-risk prediction, and asset-health monitoring, functioning as the sector's shared research layer. The IEEE Power and Energy Society publishes the underlying standards for machine learning in power systems, grid cyber-defense, and distributed energy resource management. On the subsurface side, Baker Hughes deploys AI for autonomous drilling, reservoir simulation, and pipeline monitoring, framing its portfolio explicitly around digitalization, artificial intelligence, and automation to reduce risk and drive decarbonization. Geoteric applies deep learning and computer vision to 3D seismic data to map subsurface faults for oil, gas, and geothermal exploration, and describes the technology as revolutionizing upstream exploration efforts.

Vendors concentrate at two layers. Equipment makers such as Siemens Energy deliver AI controllers and digital-twin software embedded in turbines, substations, and grid assets, meaning AI often arrives as part of a capital purchase rather than a standalone software decision. A specialist forecasting layer sits above that, with Amperon selling load, price, and renewable forecasts to utilities, traders, and asset operators, claiming accuracy up to three times better than existing solutions by processing 40,000 weather points from four vendors and analyzing roughly 25 weather variables every hour through ensemble machine learning models.

The sector occupies an unusual dual position: it is both a user of AI and AI's binding physical constraint. The DOE's 2024 Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report, tracked on this site's Power and Cooling page, found that data centers consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023 and projected that share rising to between 6.7 and 12% by 2028, with AI identified as the primary driver. DOE has responded by announcing plans to partner with private-sector developers to build AI data centers and energy-generation projects on DOE lands, and by launching a Speed to Power Initiative to accelerate large-scale grid infrastructure development.

On risk and governance, the DOE explicitly acknowledges that AI systems may generate incorrect, unverifiable, and potentially harmful outputs, and states that any use must properly understand and mitigate those risks. The department has also launched the Genesis Mission, described as combining DOE and national laboratory supercomputing, scientific data, and AI capabilities into an integrated system intended to accelerate energy independence and national security outcomes. The PermitAI tool has been released to improve federal environmental permitting speed and quality, illustrating that AI is also being applied to the regulatory process itself.

For a decision-maker weighing deployment, the sector evidence points toward well-defined use cases with measurable outputs, particularly forecasting accuracy, predictive maintenance, and subsurface interpretation, where specialist vendors and large equipment suppliers both have production deployments. The Census adoption figure's recent decline from 17.1% to 12.6% is worth noting, though the survey's scope does not capture the full industry. Federal investment through DOE and the Grid Modernization Initiative provides a relatively stable research and standards backdrop, but the same AI build-out that drives demand for energy solutions is also straining the grid infrastructure those solutions depend on.
